title: Resolving “pseudo-collaboration”: Optimizing industry-university-research cooperation motif network structures and capabilities to enhance green innovation
summary: Industry-university-research cooperation has emerged as the primary pathway for achieving green innovation breakthroughs in the new energy vehicle sector, particularly amid environmental uncertainty. However, research on how industry-university-research cooperation can resolve the “connected but not integrated” dilemma remains inadequate, particularly lacking an in-depth exploration of the paradoxical effects of meso -level motif structures and the nonlinear impacts of network capabilities. Based on network organization theory and knowledge-based theory, this study constructs a “Motif Network Structure-Capability-Performance” analytical framework. Using patent data from 803 Chinese listed new energy vehicle companies, the study combines colored network motif analysis with regression models to examine the underlying impact mechanisms through which the motif network structures and capabilities affect green innovation performance. The results indicate that: (1) motif structures exert paradoxical effects. Motifs centered on enterprises and characterized by star-like or chain-like connections positively promote green innovation performance by reducing coordination costs, whereas motifs characterized by homogeneous actor composition and arrow-shaped structures inhibit green innovation performance because of resource redundancy and elevated coordination costs; (2) the three network capabilities (knowledge acquisition, integration, and reconfiguration) exhibit U-shaped nonlinear effects characterized by a threshold effect and progressive threshold breakthrough. This research bridges the macro-micro divide in inter-organizational network studies through a meso-level motif perspective, extending network organization and knowledge-based theories to the context of industry-university-research cooperation. The conclusions provide both theoretical and practical guidance for enterprises and governments to optimize industry-university-research cooperation structures, enhance knowledge management capabilities, and develop differentiated collaborative strategies to advance green innovation.

title: Forensic Auditing and Financial Strength Transparency in Selected Southwest Government Sector of Nigeria
summary: Financial transparency, characterized by the openness, clarity, and accessibility of public financial information, remains a significant governance challenge in Southwest Nigeria. This study empirically investigates the impact of forensic auditing conceptualized through its core components of Investigative Audit Techniques (IAT), Evidence Analysis Procedures (EAP), and Litigation Support Functions (LSF) on these dimensions of transparency. Employing a quantitative research design, data was collected from 157 financial and audit professionals across state ministries in Southwest Nigeria and analyzed using multiple linear regression. The results demonstrate a differentiated impact: Openness of Financial Information (OFI) was significantly enhanced by IAT (β=0.298, p<0.01) and EAP (β=0.412, p<0.01). Clarity of Financial Disclosure (CFD) was most strongly driven by EAP (β=0.461, p<0.01), with a secondary effect from LSF (β=0.132, p<0.05). Notably, Accessibility of Financial Reporting (AFR) was positively influenced by all three components: IAT (β=0.194, p<0.01), EAP (β=0.187, p<0.05), and LSF (β=0.253, p<0.01). The regression models were statistically significant (p<0.01) with substantial explanatory power (Adjusted R²: 56.2% for OFI, 57.8% for CFD, 43.2% for AFR). The study concludes that forensic auditing is a potent but under-optimized tool for promoting transparency in the region. A critical "enforcement gap" exists, where investigative and analytical functions are more developed than the legal follow-through. We recommend the formal establishment of forensic audit units and stronger legal-institutional frameworks to ensure audit findings translate into concrete accountability and improved public financial management.

title: Digital Transformation of Municipal Waste Management in African Cities: A Socio-Technical Framework for Smart Waste Collection
summary: Rapid urbanisation and changing consumption patterns have intensified municipal solid waste-management challenges across African cities, where conventional collection is constrained by inadequate infrastructure, limited finance, irregular scheduling and weak information flows. Internet of Things (IoT) technologies offer opportunities for real-time monitoring, demand-responsive scheduling and data-supported decision-making, but technological capability alone cannot ensure successful transformation because waste management is embedded in institutional, infrastructural and social systems. This study examines the potential for digital transformation of municipal waste collection using Gwarimpa Estate, Abuja, Nigeria, as a case study and develops a socio-technical framework for implementation. A mixed-method design was employed using 380 valid household questionnaires, interviews with 20 key stakeholders and field observations. Descriptive statistics, mean scores and Relative Importance Index (RII) were used for quantitative analysis, while qualitative evidence was thematically interpreted. Respondents reported favourable expectations regarding IoT-enabled collection, particularly collection frequency (mean = 3.80; RII = 0.760), response time (mean = 3.83; RII = 0.765) and overall service improvement (mean = 3.67; RII = 0.734). Real-time monitoring and decision-making received the highest rating (mean = 4.12; RII = 0.824), while government incentives were the most highly rated implementation requirement (mean = 4.07; RII = 0.814). Electricity reliability, technical capacity, funding and internet connectivity were comparatively weaker. The study concludes that Abuja has a favourable social basis for digital transformation but requires stronger institutional and infrastructural foundations. A socio technical framework integrating technology, infrastructure, institutions, finance, operational capacity and public participation is proposed as a pathway for smart waste transformation in African cities.

title: Enterprise Architecture Leadership as a Catalyst for Digital Transformation: Influencing Strategy, Collaboration, and Change Without Formal Authority
summary: Enterprise Architecture (EA) is often associated with formal governance, architecture models, roadmaps, and future-state planning. However, many organizations benefit from EA thinking before they establish a formal EA program or dedicated EA authority. This paper explores how EA leadership can influence digital transformation, strategic planning, collaboration, and communication in organizations with maturing EA capabilities. Using Turn5, Inc., a growing e-commerce organization, as a case study, the paper analyzes academic and professional literature on EA leadership, digital transformation, agile collaboration, transformational and transactional leadership, and strategic communication. It argues that EA leaders can create value without formal authority by translating business needs into technical requirements, identifying manual processes that stunt growth, establishing stakeholder trust, and communicating how architectural transformation can influence business outcomes. This paper also explores the benefits of partnership between EA and CIO leadership, highlighting the importance of executive sponsorship and cross domain alignment in organizations where EA is informal. The case examples express the value of EA not only as a technical discipline but also as a leadership and communication role which connects people, processes, data, and utilizes technology to form executable strategy. This paper concludes that as organizations develop their EA capabilities, they should integrate architecture into agile processes, establish lightweight and dynamic governance, and develop EA leaders who can build credibility through success, collaborate across functional departments, and communicate the value of architectural change from a knowledgeable business perspective.

title: Evaluating User Experience in Accounting Software: Insights from a Multi Criteria Decision Making Approach in (COPRAS) Method
summary: Accounting software has become an important component of contemporary financial management, helping organizations efficiently monitor revenues, expenditures, and overall financial performance. These digital systems simplify accounting activities by automating functions such as invoicing, payroll processing, transaction recording, and financial reporting, thereby reducing human effort and the likelihood of errors. Different software packages serve different organizational requirements, ranging from user-friendly solutions for small businesses to advanced platforms designed for large enterprises with extensive reporting, analytical, and compliance needs. Cloud-based accounting systems further enhance flexibility by allowing financial information to be accessed remotely. Integration with other business applications also facilitates smooth data exchange and improves operational efficiency. As organizations increasingly depend on data-driven decisions, reliable accounting software has become an essential element of effective business management.Researching accounting software is important for identifying solutions that provide greater accuracy, efficiency, usability, affordability, and integration. Such evaluation assists organizations in selecting systems that support financial reporting, regulatory compliance, cost control, and long-term growth.The Complex Proportionality Assessment (COPRAS) method provides a systematic multi-criteria decision-making framework for comparing alternatives according to multiple evaluation factors. It considers the relative importance and performance of different criteria to establish an overall ranking. In this study, QuickBooks Online, Xero, FreshBooks, Sage Intacct, Zoho Books, Wave Accounting, NetSuite, and Tally ERP 9 were assessed using Ease of Use, Features, Customer Support, Price (USD/month), and Setup Time (hours). title: Knowledge-Driven reinforcement learning for Prefabricated construction supply Chain Scheduling: A Two-Phase large language model integration framework
summary: Prefabricated construction supply chains require coordinated scheduling across production, transportation, and assembly under transport uncertainty, storage constraints, and assembly precedence requirements. However, existing approaches rely on stage-isolated optimization, static heuristics, or black-box AI models that cannot ensure engineering feasibility, interpretability, and adaptive decision-making under dynamic operational conditions. To address this problem, this study proposes a knowledge-driven AI framework that formulates the three-stage scheduling problem as a Markov Decision Process and solves it using a Maskable Proximal Policy Optimization agent under a two-phase large language model integration architecture. In the offline phase, engineering constraints are extracted from technical standards via document-grounded prompt engineering, reducing manual constraint specification effort while providing traceable provenance, and embedded into reinforcement learning as action-masking predicates. In the online phase, an entropy-triggered LLM consultation mechanism provides interpretable scheduling reasoning at high-uncertainty decision points, while a Random Forest classifier enriches the reward function with delay-risk predictions to guide dispatching under weather variability. The two-phase architecture ensures that symbolic engineering knowledge constrains the action space while adaptive learning optimizes within the feasible region. Evaluated across eight scenarios spanning capacity constraints, deadline pressures, and uncertainties, the proposed framework consistently outperforms rule-based and myopic baseline policies under most scenarios. Sensitivity analysis identifies site storage capacity and dispatch batch size as dominant feasibility determinants. This study contributes a knowledge-driven and constraint-aware AI framework that bridges symbolic engineering knowledge, interpretable reasoning, and adaptive reinforcement learning for industrialized construction logistics, advancing trustworthy and uncertainty-resilient AI decision-making paradigms for complex construction supply chains.

title: Multi-objective sustainable closed-loop agricultural supply chain optimization under uncertainty respecting water circularity: olive products
summary: Abstract Driven by economic fluctuation and environmental concerns, the agricultural sector urgently requires integrated closed-loop supply chain (CLSC) models that balance profitability with sustainability. Current literature often overlooks simultaneous economic and environmental objectives, particularly concerning water circularity and reverse logistics in the olive industry. This study addresses this gap by proposing a novel bi-objective mixed integer linear programming model designed to minimize both the total supply chain cost (encompassing procurement, facility setup, operation, storage, and transportation) and total water consumption. Uncertainty regarding product yield, influenced by factors like climate and soil, is systematically incorporated using the possibilistic programming approach. The comprehensive network explicitly models forward flows, reverse logistics, package recovery, and rich wastewater utilization. This complex mathematical problem is solved using four rigorously tuned multi-objective metaheuristics (NSGA-II, NRGA, MOVNS, and MOSA). Applied to a real-world olive network case study, the model demonstrated major reductions in logistics costs, waste production, and water use. A critical finding reveals that the most impactful leverage point for water and cost efficiency lies upstream in cultivation practices (e.g., irrigation management and pest control), rather than downstream industrial recovery, providing actionable guidance for sustainable supply chain management. This research delivers a unified decision framework for water-aware CLSCs under uncertainty.

title: Stimuli in the adaptation process to digital transformation among university faculty members: internal and external drivers of technological change
summary: This study examined internal and external stimuli influencing faculty adaptation to digital transformation in higher education settings. The study applies cross-sectional survey of 154 faculty members from Kazakhstani universities used validated instruments. Results revealed a clear stimulus hierarchy: internal stimuli (intrinsic motivation, selfefficacy) explained 21% of unique variance in technology acceptance, compared to 4% for organizational support and less than 1% for external negative stimuli. External pressure showed harmful effects only among senior faculty members (β = −0.31). The cluster analysis that identified four faculty typologies characterized by distinct stimulus-response profiles. These findings suggest that successful digital transformation requires age-differentiated, autonomy-supportive institutional approaches rather than uniform mandates. The study findings can help to promote digital transformation across higher education institutions more effectively.

title: Reconceptualizing Fraud in the 21st Century: The Fraudosphere Model and Contemporary Accounting Debates
summary: This paper advances accounting theory by developing the Fraudosphere Model, a multidimensional framework that explains the evolving nature of fraud within modern financial, institutional, and technological environments. It responds to ongoing debates in accounting research regarding the theoretical adequacy of classical fraud models (the Fraud Triangle, Fraud Diamond, and Fraud Pentagon) which insufficiently capture systemic, digital, and cultural complexities shaping contemporary fraud. Using a conceptual synthesis approach, the study integrates literature from accounting, criminology, behavioral ethics, psychology, and institutional theory to construct a twelve-dimensional model emphasizing theoretical integration over empirical testing. The Fraudosphere Model identifies twelve interrelated dimensions: pressure, opportunity, rationalization, capability, arrogance, personal ethics, self-actualization, psychological triggers, cultural normalization, technological vulnerability, regulatory weakness, and perceived risk of consequences. Unlike static geometric models, the framework conceptualizes fraud as an adaptive and dynamic phenomenon operating within interdependent psychological, institutional, and technological systems. The model provides a comprehensive foundation for extending fraud risk assessment in auditing, forensic accounting, and governance. It encourages scholars and practitioners to move beyond individual-centric analyses toward systemic and contextual explanations of fraudulent behavior. Overall, the Fraudosphere Model contributes to contemporary accounting debates on the renewal of fraud theory in the digital age and establishes a basis for future empirical testing and policy application.

title: MULTI-CONTOUR PROFILE-MATRIX DIAGNOSTICS OF THE ECONOMIC RESILIENCE OF FREIGHT ROAD TRANSPORT ENTERPRISES UNDER HIGH-TECH TRANSFORMATION
summary: The article substantiates a multi-contour profile-matrix methodology for diagnosing the economic resilience of freight road transport enterprises under high-tech transformation. The approach is based on the premise that resilience cannot be reliably represented by a single integral score because strong values in one domain may conceal critical vulnerabilities in another. The proposed methodology combines five autonomous diagnostic profiles: financial-economic, operational-market, resource-technical, innovation-technological, and risk-recovery. It integrates verified data provenance, threshold zoning, dynamic indicators of resistance and recovery, cluster typology and panel modelling. A two-level information design is proposed, combining a broad panel based on official registration and financial data with an in-depth subsample containing operational and technological indicators. Four diagnostic zones—critical, vulnerable, acceptable and resilient—are used without compensatory aggregation across profiles. The methodology also distinguishes the depth of functional decline, recovery time, completeness of recovery and cumulative loss of functionality. Its practical value lies in preserving causal traceability from an observed deviation to the underlying vulnerability and in creating a direct analytical transition from diagnosis to differentiated managerial measures, scenario trajectories and investment decisions. title: The Effect of Cost of Capital, Earnings Forecast Accuracy, and Investment Efficiency on Firm Value with Analyst Coverage as a Moderating Variable
summary: This study aims to analyze the effect of cost of capital, earnings forecast accuracy, and investment efficiency on firm value, with analyst coverage as a moderating variable. Firm value is an important indicator reflecting investors' perceptions of a company's future prospects and performance. In an increasingly competitive capital market, factors influencing firm value are a primary concern for management, investors, and other stakeholders. A low cost of capital can increase firm value by optimizing funding structures and increasing profitability. Meanwhile, earnings forecast accuracy plays a role in reducing information asymmetry and increasing investor confidence in the information provided by the company. Furthermore, investment efficiency reflects a company's ability to optimally allocate resources, thereby creating added value for shareholders. This study also examines the role of analyst coverage as a moderating variable, which is expected to strengthen or weaken the relationship between the independent variables and firm value. The greater the analyst coverage of a company, the greater the quality of information available in the market, thereby increasing the effectiveness of the influence of cost of capital, earnings forecast accuracy, and investment efficiency on firm value. The results of this study are expected to provide theoretical contributions to the field of corporate finance and serve as a consideration for investors and management in strategic decision-making.

title: The Determinant of Sustainability Report Disclosure (SRD) in companies listed on the LQ45 Index on the Indonesia Stock Exchange
summary: The purpose of this study is to objectively investigate the impact of independent commissioners, gender representation on the Board of Directors (BoD), media exposure, and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) on Sustainability Report Disclosure (SRD). This study's population consists of companies listed in the LQ45 index on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) between 2021 and 2023, for a total of 135 units of analysis, with 89 final units. The research sample was selected using a purposive sampling method. This study used panel data regression analysis with EViews 12 Student Lite and the Random Effects Model (REM). The study's findings indicate that independent commissioners have no effect on SRD. Gender representation on the Board of Directors has a considerable detrimental impact on SRD. Media exposure has a considerable favourable impact on SRD. Meanwhile, ESG has a strong favourable impact on SRD. This study examines the effects of independent commissioners, gender representation on the board of directors, media exposure, and ESG on SRD. The use of ESG as a variable is deemed new, given it is rarely used in SRD studies. This analysis has drawbacks, as the independent commissioner variable had no significant influence, implying that different proxies could be utilized. To increase the adjusted R-squared, future research should include variables such as audit committee, foreign ownership, and family ownership.

title: Financial resources ecological orientation and capabilities as antecedents of environmental management accounting for sustainable competitive advantage
summary: Environmental Management Accounting (EMA) enables SMEs to adopt greener production practices and strengthen their sustainable competitive advantage (SCA). While EMA is recognized for enhancing performance in large firms, significant research gaps persist regarding its application within small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), particularly in new geographical contexts. Prior studies acknowledge the role of antecedents of EMA, whether tangible or intangible resources. However, limited research simultaneously examines both types of resources alongside organizational capabilities to determine EMA adoption. This study addresses the limited empirical evidence on the combined role of financial resources (FR), natural ecological orientation (NEO), and environmental innovation capabilities (EIC) as key antecedents to EMA adoption. It further examines the mediating effect of EMA adoption on SCA among manufacturing SMEs in Kenya. Grounded in the natural resource-based view (NRBV), data were collected from 206 SMEs and analyzed using SmartPLS 4. Empirical findings indicate no significant relationship between FR and EMA adoption, supporting the argument that intangible resources may be more instrumental than tangible resources in fostering SCA through EMA. In contrast, NEO and EIC demonstrated strong and significant relationships with EMA adoption. Additionally, results show that EMA adoption significantly enhances SCA, with NEO and EIC exerting significant positive effects on SCA through EMA adoption. Practically, the findings guide SMEs in leveraging NEO and EIC to boost green performance and value within global supply chains by creating shared sustainability benefits beyond compliance. Furthermore, the study informs policymakers on how to promote these enablers to enhance SME competitiveness in sustainable markets.

title: Auditing Dynamical Claims An Executable Audit Protocol for Separating Causal Manifestation, Finite-Sample Detection, and Classification
summary: Auditing Dynamical Claims presents an executable protocol for preventing scientific claims about dynamical systems from being strengthened beyond what the design and evidence actually support. The protocol separates several evidential layers that are often conflated: mechanistic presence, representation stability, causal manifestation at a declared interface, temporal equivalence, finite-sample condition detection, case-level classification, and countermodel or triangulation status. Researchers specify these elements in advance through a structured claim tuple, and an accompanying machine-readable schema and Python checker return an evidence vector, allowed claims, blocked claims, and a conservative claim ceiling. The protocol is designed as an integration and reporting layer over existing methods rather than as a replacement for observability, identifiability, causal inference, sequential testing, or model-validation theory. The paper demonstrates the framework in two settings. A controlled fresh-seed synthetic benchmark shows that the same causal manifestation time can produce very different finite-sample detection probabilities and classification performance when only noise and sample budget change. An external observational demonstration using the Nile annual-flow series shows the complementary case: a strong statistical level shift can be supported while causal attribution remains blocked because the required intervention or counterfactual design is absent. The contribution is procedural rather than mathematical: a machine-readable claim-audit workflow for exposing unsupported inferential transitions and keeping the final reported claim at the strongest level actually licensed by the available evidence.

title: Unravelling the minefield of audit transgressions and sanctions
summary: Background: Audit failures undermine public trust and investor confidence. The Independent Regulatory Board for Auditors (IRBA) is tasked with ensuring that regulatory audits comply with International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) and helping prevent failures by issuing sanctions for transgressions. In contrast, auditors tend to make similar mistakes repeatedly, indicating a research gap regarding the types of transgressions that result in IRBA sanctions. Aim: This study investigates the types of audit transgressions and the repercussions of these transgressions on the severity of IRBA sanctions. Setting: This study examines 923 audit transgressions from 01 January 2019 to 30 June 2025, and the 405 sanctions IRBA imposed to punish auditors for transgressions. Method: Firstly, a retrospective document analysis of the types of audit transgressions was conducted. Secondly, a multivariable regression analysis was conducted to assess the likely repercussions of the various types of transgressions on the severity of imposed sanctions. Results: Most sanctions related to non-compliance with the independence requirements of the IRBA Code and to auditors failing to obtain sufficient and appropriate audit evidence as required by ISA 500. Transgressions relating to non-compliance with Section 38(3) and 41(6)(e) of the Auditing Profession Act, Rules 2.6 and 2.7 of the Rules regarding improper conduct and ISA 705 were most influential on the value of sanctions imposed. Conclusion: The focal point of this study is to highlight the nature of past transgressions that have resulted in IRBA sanctions, so that audit practitioners can avoid similar transgressions. Contribution: This study provides valuable insights for practitioners, offering guidance on avoiding pitfalls that have led to past sanctions.

title: The Influence of Capital Structure and Institutional Ownership on Firm Value with CSR as a Moderating Variable
summary: This study aims to examine the influence of capital structure and institutional ownership on firm value, with Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as a moderating variable, in manufacturing companies within the basic and chemical industries subsector listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the period 2020–2024. This study employs a quantitative method using secondary data obtained from companies’ annual reports and sustainability reports. The sampling technique employed purposive sampling, resulting in 26 companies selected as the research sample, comprising a total of 130 observations. The data analysis techniques used were multiple linear regression and Moderated Regression Analysis (MRA) using SPSS version 25. The results indicate that capital structure has a significant effect on firm value. Institutional ownership also has a significant effect on firm value. Furthermore, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has a significant effect on firm value. However, CSR is unable to moderate the relationship between capital structure and firm value, nor the relationship between institutional ownership and firm value. These findings suggest that investors still view high levels of debt and CSR disclosures as factors that can increase a firm’s financial burden, thereby leading to a decline in firm value.

title: THEORETICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS OF THE INTERNAL AUDIT OF RECEIVABLES AND PAYABLES IN BUDGET ORGANIZATIONS
summary: The article develops a theoretical and methodological framework for the internal audit of receivables and payables in budget (public sector) organizations. The author argues that in the public sector these categories cannot be interpreted through the logic of commercial capital circulation: a receivable represents a temporary immobilisation of budget resources, while a payable is, in the typical case, the accounting trace of an obligation assumed in excess of an approved appropriation limit. Consequently, the audit objective shifts from the fair presentation of balances towards the legality, economy and controllability of the obligation cycle. Drawing on the COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework, the IIA professional framework, INTOSAI public sector guidance and the accrual-based IPSAS model, a three-level methodological construct is proposed: the conceptual level (object, subject, purpose, principles), the organisational-institutional level (mandate, independence, three lines model) and the procedural-instrumental level (risk assessment, materiality, assertion-mapped procedures, key risk indicators). The study concludes that the transition from a compliance-verification model to a risk-based assurance model constitutes the central methodological problem of internal audit in the budget sphere.

title: Design and Development of a Website-Based Accounting Information System Using the Laravel Framework for the Nasi Kuning Angel Msme
summary: This study aims to design and develop a web-based sales accounting information system using the Laravel framework to address the lack of structured financial record-keeping at the MSME "Nasi Kuning Angel." Previously, the absence of such a system hindered the owner from evaluating business performance and preparing the financial reports often required for external financing applications. The study employs the Waterfall development methodology, encompassing the stages of requirements analysis, system design, implementation, testing, and maintenance. The system design utilizes Use Case Diagrams and Activity Diagrams, which are technically implemented via the Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture in Laravel. The results demonstrate the successful development of a system featuring a public landing page, transaction journal recording, a general ledger, and automated financial dashboards and reports. Testing conducted using Use Case Testing techniques confirms that all operational functions and authorization validations operate correctly in accordance with user requirement specifications. This web application modernizes the MSME's administrative management, facilitates transaction recording, and generates standard-compliant profit and loss statements and trial balances.

title: Self-Control and Fintech Adoption in Mediating the Effect of Social Capital on Responsible Financial Behavior
summary: The rapid growth of fintech in Indonesia has improved access to digital financial services, but this has not automatically translated into more responsible financial behavior, particularly among Millennials balancing family, credit, and career obligations. This study examines how social capital influences responsible financial behavior among Millennials in Pontianak City, both directly and through the mediating roles of self-control and fintech adoption. A quantitative survey was distributed to Millennial respondents (born 1981–1996) domiciled in Pontianak, yielding 205 valid responses, analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). The results show that social capital significantly and positively influences self-control, fintech adoption, and responsible financial behavior directly, while self-control and fintech adoption jointly and sequentially mediate the effect of social capital on responsible financial behavior. All six hypothesized relationships were statistically supported. The findings indicate that fintech adoption serves as a behavioral mechanism through which social and psychological capital translate into financial conduct, with self-control playing the dominant mediating role. These results extend behavioral finance literature to an underrepresented regional and generational context and offer practical implications for fintech providers, financial educators, and policymakers seeking to strengthen responsible financial behavior among Millennials.

title: Beyond CSR Expenditure: Reconceptualising ESG-Based Corporate Sustainability Governance in India
summary: With the Companies Act of 2013, India became the first country to impose CSR expenditure requirements on companies. While spending on CSR has steadily increased in India, the impact of CSR on environmental activities has remained limited. This paper compares the environmental CSR structure in the country with the ESG based governance structure in the UK where more emphasis is put on the need for sustainability reporting, accountability to stakeholders and having specific results of the implemented projects. The study employs a doctrinal and socio-legal methodology in order to review statutory provisions, various policy papers, CSR data and sustainability reports by Tata Steel, Reliance Industries, NTPC Limited, Infosys, and Mahindra Group. The findings show that environmental projects get a small part of the total CSR budget and that companies tend to implement quick and visual projects most of the time. The main challenges include the lack of proper impact assessment, imbalance between regions, fragmentation of regulation, and symbolic compliance. The paper concludes that India should move further than just compliance based on the amount spent and adopt a more outcome and ESG focused approach.

title: Disclosing environment-focused SDGs in emerging markets: the role of climate governance and contextual moderators
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how climate governance influences corporate disclosure of environment-focused sustainable development goals (En_SDGs) in emerging Asian economies, where firms face increasing pressure to address climate risks and environmental accountability. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on stakeholder, resource dependence and signalling theories, the study analyses 300 large non-financial firms over the period 2016–17 to 2021–22. A climate governance index (CGINX) is constructed using six governance mechanisms, while En_SDGs disclosure is measured through content analysis based on the global reporting initiative framework. The hypotheses are tested using a panel Tobit model. Findings The results show that climate governance is positively associated with En_SDGs disclosure, indicating that structured governance mechanisms facilitate more extensive and credible environmental reporting. The findings further reveal that this relationship is strengthened by firm profitability and national carbon emission intensity, suggesting that both internal resource capacity and external environmental pressure condition the effectiveness of climate governance. Robustness checks confirm the stability of these results. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of strengthening climate governance and supportive institutional environments to enhance environmental transparency, providing relevant insights for firms, investors, regulators and policymakers. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by linking climate governance to SDG-specific environmental disclosure in an emerging market context and by demonstrating that governance effectiveness varies across firm- and country-level conditions.
